title: DevOps & DevSecOps
subtitle: The 8-step CI/CD infinite loop from Plan to Monitor, and integrating security throughout via CVE tracking, OWASP, SAST/DAST, and secret scanning.
contentMarkdown:
## DevOps & DevSecOps — IT, Development, and Security Combined

---

## Part A: Introduction to DevOps

### 1. The CI/CD Infinite Loop

DevOps is commonly visualized as an **infinite loop** of eight phases, split into two halves:

- **CI (Continuous Integration) half:** Plan → Code → Build → Test
- **CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) half:** Release → Deploy → Operate → Monitor

The loop is continuous — insights from Monitor feed back into the next Plan phase, and the cycle repeats indefinitely rather than ending at "deploy."

### 2. Step 1 — Plan

Planning happens in a work-tracking tool (e.g. Azure DevOps Boards) as a structured work item — a user story with:
- A **description** written from the user's perspective (e.g. "As an authenticated user, I want to see all my accounts and their balances on a dashboard"), including acceptance criteria embedded in the description (e.g. "API call failure shows user-friendly error; page loads within 2 seconds").
- **Planning fields**: story points, priority, and risk — used to estimate and prioritize the work.
- **Classification** fields (e.g. value area: Business) linking the technical task back to business value.
- Direct links from the work item to its **development** (commits/pull requests/branches) and **deployment** (release tracking), so planning, code, and delivery stay traceable to each other.

### 3. Step 2 — Code

Developers implement the planned work in an IDE, typically organizing the solution into clearly-separated services/layers (e.g. an `AccountService`, `PaymentService`, `TransactionService`, each split into Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and Api projects — a layered/domain-driven structure). Code here directly implements the acceptance criteria defined in the Plan step (e.g. a `SendPaymentCommandHandler` that validates a recipient account before creating a payment).

### 4. Step 3 — Build

The build step compiles the solution and restores dependencies — but a build is also where **dependency vulnerability scanning** naturally surfaces, because package managers (e.g. NuGet) can flag known-vulnerable dependencies automatically during restore:

```
warning NU1903: Package 'System.Security.Cryptography.Xml' 9.0 has a known high severity vulnerability
warning NU1902: Package 'OpenTelemetry.Api' 1.11.2 has a known moderate severity vulnerability
```

This is a concrete example of **security shifting left**: a real CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) in a third-party dependency is surfaced automatically during a routine build, long before the vulnerable code would ever reach production — the developer sees the warning the moment they build locally or in CI, not after a security audit months later.

### 5. Step 4 — Test

Automated tests run via a test runner (e.g. Visual Studio's Test Explorer), reporting pass/fail counts per test group (e.g. "118 passed, 0 failed"). Testing also covers **input validation** at the UI layer — e.g. a "Send Payment" form rejecting an invalid recipient account number ("Enter a valid 7-digit account number") before the request is even submitted, mirroring the constraints-based validation principle from UI/UX design.

### 6. Step 5 — Release

Releasing is the step where a new version is prepared to go live, without yet being exposed to users. A common pattern (shown via container "pods" in a cluster):

- **Active running pods (live to end users):** the current version (e.g. `v1.2.3`) continues serving all live traffic.
- **Pods being created (not live to end users yet):** new pods running the next version (e.g. `v1.2.4`) are started up **in parallel**, but are **not yet receiving user traffic**.

New pods are created and started in the cluster; **they are not live to end users until traffic is switched.** This separation of "started" from "live" is what allows a release to be validated (health checks, smoke tests) before it's actually exposed — and allows an instant rollback (just don't switch traffic, or switch it back) if something is wrong, without needing to redeploy.

### 7. Step 6 — Deploy

Deploy is the step where traffic is actually switched to the new version — the point at which the newly-released pods stop being "not live" and start actually serving real users.

### 8. Step 7 — Operate

Once deployed, the system runs live in production, serving real users performing real actions — e.g. a live banking app where users view account dashboards, transfer funds between their own accounts, and send payments to other accounts. This is the system actually doing its job in the real world, not just passing tests in a controlled environment.

### 9. Step 8 — Monitor

Monitoring closes the loop by observing the running system from two complementary angles:

- **Technical/distributed tracing** (e.g. via Jaeger): individual requests are broken into **traces** made up of **spans** — e.g. a trace for `PaymentService: POST /api/v1/payments` shows exactly how long the request took and which downstream services (`AccountService`, `PaymentService`) it touched, letting engineers pinpoint exactly where latency or errors occur across service boundaries.
- **User behaviour analytics** (e.g. heatmaps, session replay, funnels): tools can show where users actually click, scroll, and spend attention on a live page (a heatmap), replay entire user sessions, and track engagement metrics — connecting the technical health of the system to how real users are actually experiencing it.

The insights from monitoring — a slow trace, a confusing UI heatmap, a recurring error — feed directly back into the next **Plan** phase, closing the infinite loop.

---

## Part B: Introduction to DevSecOps

DevSecOps means **security is integrated throughout the entire DevOps loop**, not bolted on as a separate final gate — security becomes part of Plan, Code, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate, and Monitor, not a step that only happens right before (or after) release.

### 1. CVE — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures

**CVE** is a publicly maintained, community-driven catalogue of publicly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerabilities — each one assigned a standard CVE identifier so that different tools, vendors, and researchers can all refer to the *same* vulnerability unambiguously. This is the exact mechanism behind the build-time warnings seen in Step 3 (`NU1903`, `NU1902`) — package ecosystems cross-reference dependency versions against CVE-style vulnerability databases to warn developers automatically.

### 2. OWASP — Open Web Application Security Project

**OWASP** is a well-known open community focused on web application security, best known for resources like the **OWASP Top 10** — a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks (e.g. injection, broken access control, security misconfiguration) used industry-wide as a baseline for what to defend against.

### 3. Tooling: DAST vs. SAST

Two complementary categories of automated security testing tooling:

- **SAST (Static Application Security Testing)** — analyzes source code (or compiled bytecode) **without running it**, looking for known-insecure patterns directly in the code (e.g. string-concatenated SQL queries, hardcoded credentials, use of unsafe functions). Runs early — can be part of the Build/Code step, catching issues before the application ever executes.
- **DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing)** — tests a **running** application from the outside, the way an attacker would: sending malicious/unexpected inputs to a live running instance and observing the actual responses/behaviour, to catch vulnerabilities that only manifest at runtime (e.g. in how the app actually handles a crafted request), which static analysis of the source code alone can miss.

### 4. Secret Scanning

Automated scanning (of source code, commit history, and configuration files) for accidentally committed secrets — API keys, passwords, tokens, private keys — before or immediately after they land in a repository. This directly mirrors the "secrets do not belong in your repo" principle from L17's CI/CD material: secret scanning is the *automated tooling* that catches this class of mistake as part of the DevSecOps pipeline, rather than relying on developers to never make it.

mcqs.explanation: SAST is static (code, not running); DAST is dynamic (a live running instance, tested externally).

mcqs.q: Why can DAST catch vulnerabilities that SAST might miss?
options: DAST is always faster to run than SAST
DAST observes actual runtime behaviour by testing a live running application, catching issues that only manifest when the code is actually executing
DAST doesn't require any application to be running

mcqs.q: What does secret scanning specifically look for?

Accidentally committed secrets — API keys, passwords, tokens, private keys — in source code, commit history, or config files

mcqs.explanation: This distribution directly reflects DevSecOps' core idea: security integrated at every phase, each tool suited to where it can act earliest and most effectively.

techQuestions.q: Using the build output shown in the lecture (the NU1903 and NU1902 warnings), explain step by step how a CVE in a third-party dependency ends up surfaced to a developer as a build warning, and why this is a practical example of "shifting security left."
techQuestions.answer:
**Step by step:**
1. A researcher or the community discovers a vulnerability in a published package (e.g. `System.Security.Cryptography.Xml`) and it is catalogued with a standard CVE identifier, along with a severity rating (high/moderate/etc.) and an advisory describing the issue.
2. Package registries (e.g. NuGet, npm) maintain or consume a database that cross-references published package versions against known CVE advisories.
3. When a developer runs a build, the package manager step (`dotnet restore` / `yarn install` under the hood) resolves the project's dependency tree to specific package versions, and checks each resolved version against that advisory database.
4. If a resolved version matches a known vulnerability, the build tooling emits a warning directly in the build output — exactly the `NU1903`/`NU1902` lines shown, including a link to the advisory — without the developer having to do anything beyond a normal build.

**Why this is "shifting left":** "Shifting left" means moving a check earlier in the pipeline (visually, toward the left/start of the pipeline diagram) instead of leaving it for the end. Here, a vulnerability that might otherwise only be discovered during a dedicated security audit — potentially months after the vulnerable dependency was introduced, and possibly after it has already shipped to production — is instead surfaced the moment *any* developer runs *any* normal build, whether locally on their laptop or in CI. The cost of fixing it (bumping a package version) is trivial at this point; the cost of fixing the same vulnerability after it's been running in production for months (incident response, patching under pressure, potentially a breach) is dramatically higher. Shifting the check left doesn't change *what* is found — it changes *when*, catching the same problem while it's still cheap.

techQuestions.q: Explain the operational difference between the Release step and the Deploy step in this lecture's model, using the pod diagram. Why might a team choose to treat these as two distinct steps rather than one?
techQuestions.answer:
**The difference:** in the Release step, new pods running the next version (e.g. `v1.2.4`) are **created and started** inside the cluster, running alongside the currently-active pods (`v1.2.3`) — but they receive **zero live user traffic** at this point; they exist and are running, but are not yet "live." In the Deploy step, traffic is actually **switched** to those already-running new pods — this is the moment they transition from "exists but idle" to "actually serving real users."

**Why treat them as two distinct steps:**
1. **Validation window.** Once the new pods are started (Release) but before any real user traffic reaches them (before Deploy), the team has an opportunity to run health checks, smoke tests, or synthetic traffic against the new version in a real, running environment — without any risk to real users, since nothing user-facing depends on those pods yet.
2. **Fast, low-risk rollback.** If Deploy (the traffic switch) reveals a problem, rolling back is as simple as switching traffic back to the still-running old pods — no redeploy, no rebuild, near-instant recovery. If Release and Deploy were the same atomic step (new pods immediately take over serving traffic the instant they start), any problem discovered after the fact requires either an emergency rollback deployment or user-facing downtime while it's fixed forward.
3. **Decoupling "is it ready" from "is it live."** Splitting these lets a team treat "the new version exists and is running correctly" and "users are now using the new version" as two separate, independently-controllable facts — which is exactly what enables techniques like canary releases (route only a fraction of traffic to the new pods) or blue-green deployments (switch all traffic at once, but only when ready).

techQuestions.q: A team's monitoring dashboard shows a Jaeger trace revealing that a `POST /api/v1/payments` request spends 90% of its total duration inside a call to `AccountService`. Explain how this observation flows back into the Plan step of the next loop iteration, and what kind of work item might result.
techQuestions.answer:
**How it flows back:** the DevOps loop is explicitly closed — Monitor's output is not a dead end, it's the input to the next Plan phase. A trace showing that 90% of a payment request's latency is concentrated in one specific downstream call (`AccountService`) is a precise, evidence-based signal about *where* the system's actual bottleneck is, as opposed to a vague complaint like "payments feel slow." This is exactly the kind of concrete finding that turns into a planned, prioritized piece of work rather than being lost or forgotten, because it's backed by measured data rather than guesswork.

**What kind of work item might result:** a new backlog item would likely be created in the Plan step — structured the same way as the lecture's example work item — something like:

> **User Story:** As a user, I want the payment submission flow to respond quickly, so that I don't experience a slow, unresponsive UI when sending a payment.
> **Description / Acceptance Criteria:** `POST /api/v1/payments` should complete in under [target] ms at the 95th percentile; specifically investigate and reduce the AccountService call latency identified in trace [link], which currently accounts for ~90% of total request duration.
> **Planning fields:** Priority — high (if this affects a critical user-facing path); Story points — estimated once the root cause inside AccountService (e.g. a slow query, a missing cache, a synchronous call that could be made async) is investigated.

The key point: the trace doesn't just report *that* something's slow — it tells the team specifically *where* to look, which turns an abstract performance concern into an actionable, scoped, prioritizable planning item, exactly the kind of concrete input the Plan step is meant to consume.

techQuestions.q: Compare SAST and DAST directly: for a SQL injection vulnerability that exists in application code but is protected behind an authentication check that a scanner can't pass, which tool is more likely to catch it, and why?
techQuestions.answer:
**SAST** analyzes source code (or compiled bytecode) directly, without executing the application — it looks for known-dangerous *patterns* in the code itself, such as a database query built via string concatenation with unsanitized user input. Because SAST reads the code as text/structure rather than running it, it does **not** need to authenticate, log in, or navigate through the application at all — it can see the vulnerable query construction directly in the source, regardless of what access control sits in front of the endpoint at runtime.

**DAST** tests a **live, running** application from the outside, behaving like an external attacker sending real HTTP requests and observing real responses. Critically, DAST can only test what it can actually *reach* — if the vulnerable endpoint sits behind an authentication check that the DAST scanner's automated crawler can't pass (e.g. it doesn't have valid test credentials configured, or the login flow uses something the scanner can't automate, like a CAPTCHA or MFA), the scanner will simply never reach the vulnerable code path at all, and will report no finding — not because the vulnerability doesn't exist, but because the tool never got past the front door.

**Which tool is more likely to catch this specific case:** **SAST**. Since SAST reads the vulnerable query-construction code directly from the source, the authentication barrier is irrelevant to it — SAST doesn't need to "get past" anything to see the code. DAST, by contrast, is entirely dependent on being able to actually exercise the vulnerable code path at runtime; if it can't authenticate, it can't test the protected endpoint at all, and the vulnerability would go undetected by DAST alone in this scenario. This is exactly why DevSecOps typically uses SAST and DAST **together**, as complementary tools with different blind spots, rather than relying on either one alone.

techQuestions.q: Design a DevSecOps-integrated version of the standard 8-step DevOps loop by mapping at least one specific security practice (from CVE checking, OWASP Top 10 awareness, SAST, DAST, or secret scanning) onto each of the 8 steps.
techQuestions.answer:
1. **Plan** — Threat-model the feature against the **OWASP Top 10** as part of writing acceptance criteria (e.g. for a login feature, explicitly plan for "broken access control" and "injection" risks up front, not as an afterthought).
2. **Code** — Use an IDE-integrated **SAST** linter/plugin that flags insecure patterns (e.g. string-concatenated SQL, hardcoded secrets) as the developer types, before the code is even committed.
3. **Build** — Run automated **dependency/CVE scanning** during package restore (exactly the NU1903/NU1902 pattern shown in the lecture) and **secret scanning** on the diff being built, failing the build on critical findings.
4. **Test** — Run a full **SAST** pass across the entire codebase (not just changed files) as a CI stage, and include security-specific test cases (e.g. attempting SQL injection payloads against test endpoints) alongside functional tests.
5. **Release** — Run **DAST** against the newly-started (but not-yet-live) pods from the Release step's staging environment — exactly the validation window the pod diagram creates — catching runtime-only vulnerabilities before any real traffic is switched to them.
6. **Deploy** — Verify the deployed artefact's **signature and SBOM** (tying back to L17's supply-chain security material) before allowing the traffic switch to proceed, ensuring the exact artefact that was scanned is the one going live.
7. **Operate** — Run continuous, scheduled **DAST** scans and dependency **CVE** re-checks against the live production system, since new CVEs can be disclosed for dependencies that were "clean" at deploy time.
8. **Monitor** — Feed security-relevant signals (e.g. anomalous traffic patterns, repeated failed auth attempts visible in traces/logs) into monitoring dashboards alongside performance data, so security incidents are detected with the same observability tooling (e.g. Jaeger-style tracing) used for performance issues, and loop back into the next Plan phase as prioritized security work.

techQuestions.q: Explain why "not live until traffic is switched" (the Release step's pod separation) is a form of risk mitigation. What could go wrong if a team's deployment process didn't have this separation, and pods went live to users the instant they started?
techQuestions.answer:
**Why it's risk mitigation:** the separation converts deployment from a single, all-or-nothing, irreversible event into two independently-controllable steps: "does the new version start up and run correctly" (Release) and "should real users actually be using it" (Deploy). Because the second question can be answered — via health checks, smoke tests, or simply watching the new pods for errors — *before* any real user is affected, the team gets a genuine opportunity to catch a broken deployment with zero user-facing impact, and to reverse course (simply not switching traffic, or switching it back) without any redeploy at all.

**What could go wrong without this separation:** if a pod becomes "live" the instant it starts, then any problem in the new version — a missing environment variable, a failed database migration, a crash-on-startup bug, a subtly broken business logic change — is discovered *by real users hitting it in production*, not by the team in a controlled check. Consider a scenario where `v1.2.4` has a bug causing every payment request to silently fail: without the Release/Deploy separation, the moment the new pods start, they'd begin receiving live payment traffic and failing real user transactions immediately, with no window in which the team could have caught this via a smoke test first. Recovery would then require either scrambling to redeploy the previous version under pressure (itself a re-run of the full pipeline, taking real time during which the bug is actively affecting users) or, worse, if pods are being replaced one-by-one without careful traffic control, a confusing partial-failure state where *some* requests hit the broken new version and others hit the still-running old version — exactly the kind of production incident this two-step separation is specifically designed to prevent.

techQuestions.q: A recipient account number validation error ("Enter a valid 7-digit account number") appears in the Test step's example. Explain how this specific UI behaviour demonstrates both a software testing concept (from L19) and a UI/UX design concept (from L20) simultaneously.
techQuestions.answer:
**As a software testing concept (L19):** this behaviour is most directly a **functional test** concern — "does this feature behave as intended?" Specifically, it's testing input validation logic: given an account number that doesn't match the required 7-digit format, does the system correctly reject it and communicate why, rather than silently accepting bad data or crashing? A test suite would cover this with explicit test cases: valid 7-digit input → accepted; too-short input → rejected with the specific error message; non-numeric input → rejected; etc. This is exactly the kind of behaviour a well-named, well-designed test (per L19's "implementing tests" guidance) would verify and document.

**As a UI/UX design concept (L20):** the same behaviour is simultaneously a **constraint**, in L20's terms — the interface prevents (or at minimum immediately flags) an invalid action rather than silently accepting bad input and failing later, deeper in the system (e.g. only discovering the invalid account number after attempting to process the payment against a non-existent account). The specific, actionable error message ("Enter a valid 7-digit account number," rather than a generic "Error") also reflects L20's discoverability and feedback principles: the user immediately knows *what* was wrong and *what* a valid input looks like, rather than being left to guess.

**Why this matters as a single example demonstrating both:** it shows that testing and UX design aren't separate concerns bolted onto different parts of the system — the *same* piece of validation logic simultaneously satisfies "does the feature behave correctly" (a testing concern, verified by automated tests) and "does the user understand what went wrong and how to fix it" (a UX concern, evaluated by how the error is communicated). A good implementation has to get both right: the validation must be logically correct (testable, verifiable) *and* the resulting user-facing message must be clear and actionable (well-designed) — one without the other is an incomplete solution.

techQuestions.q: Explain why CVE identifiers being "standardized" matters in practice — what would go wrong in dependency vulnerability scanning (like the NuGet warnings shown) if there were no shared, standard vulnerability identifiers across the industry?
techQuestions.answer:
A CVE identifier acts as a **universal, unambiguous reference** for a specific vulnerability — every tool, vendor, researcher, and package registry that references "CVE-2024-XXXXX" is guaranteed to be talking about the exact same underlying issue, regardless of which company or team discovered it, which language ecosystem it affects, or which scanning tool is checking for it.

**What would go wrong without this standardization:** imagine instead that every security research group, every package registry (NuGet, npm, PyPI), and every scanning vendor maintained its own independent, differently-formatted vulnerability catalogue with its own internal naming scheme. The specific automated check shown in the lecture — NuGet's package restore step automatically cross-referencing a resolved package version against a vulnerability database and emitting a `NU1903` warning — depends entirely on that database being able to say, unambiguously, "package X at version Y has vulnerability Z, described here." Without a shared identifier:
- The same real-world vulnerability might be independently rediscovered and separately catalogued multiple times under different names by different organizations, making it impossible to know if two advisories from different sources describe the same issue or two different ones.
- Tooling built by one vendor (e.g. GitHub's dependency scanning) couldn't reliably cross-reference findings with tooling built by another vendor (e.g. NuGet's built-in restore-time check, or a separate SAST/dependency-scanning product), since they'd have no common key to match records against.
- A developer seeing a warning would have no reliable way to search for more information, check if a fix already exists, or confirm whether the specific version they're using is actually patched — every source might describe "the same" issue slightly differently, with no canonical reference to reconcile them.

In short, CVE's standardization is precisely what makes automated, cross-tool, cross-vendor vulnerability detection like the lecture's NuGet build warnings *possible* at scale — it's the shared vocabulary the entire ecosystem of security tooling depends on to interoperate.

techQuestions.q: A company currently only runs DAST scans once a year during a scheduled external penetration test. Using DevSecOps principles from the lecture, explain what's wrong with this approach and how it should be integrated into the pipeline instead.
techQuestions.answer:
**What's wrong:** this is the exact opposite of the DevSecOps principle the lecture defines — security integrated *throughout* the loop, not as a single, infrequent, end-of-cycle gate. An annual DAST scan means that any vulnerability introduced by a code change has, on average, up to a year of exposure in production before it's ever detected by this process — during which the vulnerable code may have shipped multiple releases, been exercised by real (and potentially malicious) traffic, and had its blast radius grow as more features are built on top of the vulnerable component. It also means that when a vulnerability *is* found during the annual test, it could take significant investigative effort just to identify *which* of potentially dozens of releases over the past year introduced it, since there's no fine-grained, per-change signal — only one snapshot per year.

**How it should be integrated instead:** per the lecture's Release step, DAST should run against the system in an environment that mirrors production but isn't yet receiving live traffic — i.e., DAST against the newly-started (but not-yet-deployed) pods, before the Deploy step switches real traffic to them. This means every release candidate gets scanned, not just once a year — catching a newly-introduced vulnerability within a single release cycle (days/weeks) rather than up to twelve months later, and narrowing the "which change caused this" investigation down to a single release's diff instead of a year's worth of changes. The annual external penetration test doesn't need to be eliminated — it still adds value as an independent, deeper, human-led check — but it should be a *supplement* to continuous, automated, per-release DAST, not a substitute for it, exactly matching DevSecOps' principle of security running throughout the loop rather than concentrated at one infrequent gate.

techQuestions.q: Explain the relationship between distributed tracing (Jaeger, shown in Monitor) and the microservices architecture concepts from L18. Why does distributed tracing become necessary specifically in a microservices architecture in a way it wouldn't be for a monolith?
techQuestions.answer:
**In a monolith:** a single incoming request (e.g. processing a payment) executes as one continuous call stack within a single process. If something is slow or fails, a developer can typically get a complete picture just by reading a single stack trace or a single process's logs — every step of handling that request happened inside one process, in one place, with one execution context.

**In a microservices architecture (per L18):** the same logical operation — "process this payment" — is decomposed into a call that spans multiple, independently-deployed services communicating over the network (e.g. a request to `PaymentService`, which in turn calls `AccountService` to verify balance and update account state). Each service has its own process, its own logs, and — critically — its own independent execution context. A single logical request now has no single call stack to read; it's scattered across N separate services' logs, each of which only sees its own piece of the interaction, with no inherent way to tell which log lines across different services correspond to the *same* originating request.

**Why distributed tracing becomes necessary:** distributed tracing solves exactly this problem by propagating a shared trace ID across every service boundary a single logical request crosses, and recording each service's contribution as a "span" within that shared trace. This is what lets the lecture's Jaeger example show that a single `POST /api/v1/payments` request touched both `PaymentService` and `AccountService`, and exactly how long each one took — reconstructing, after the fact, the same complete picture that a monolith's single call stack would have given you "for free," but which the microservices architecture's decentralized, independently-deployed services structurally cannot provide without this extra tracing infrastructure. This is a direct, practical consequence of the "decentralized control" and "independent deployment" characteristics L18 attributes to microservices — the same properties that give microservices their benefits (independent scaling, independent deployment) are exactly what make simple, monolith-style debugging (read one process's log) insufficient, and dedicated cross-service observability tooling like Jaeger a practical necessity rather than a nice-to-have.

techQuestions.q: Using the lecture's user behaviour analytics tools (heatmaps, session replay, funnels) shown in Monitor, explain how these tools could reveal a UI/UX problem (per L20's concepts) that a purely technical monitoring tool like Jaeger would never surface, and vice versa.
techQuestions.answer:
**What Jaeger (technical tracing) can and cannot see:** Jaeger measures *system* behaviour — request latency, which services were called, whether calls succeeded or failed. It has no concept of what a user was actually trying to accomplish or how they felt about the interaction. A request can be technically perfect by every metric Jaeger tracks — fast, error-free, all downstream calls succeeding — while the user experience built on top of that request is still confusing or frustrating. For example: a checkout API call that returns a `200 OK` in 80ms (excellent by Jaeger's metrics) could still power a confirmation screen that, per L20's feedback principles, gives the user no visible confirmation that anything happened — Jaeger would show a perfectly healthy trace for an interaction the user experienced as "did that even work?"

**What heatmaps/session replay/funnels can and cannot see:** these tools directly capture what L20's material is actually about — where users click, how far they scroll, where they hesitate, and at what step in a multi-step flow they abandon it (a funnel drop-off). A heatmap could reveal that users are repeatedly clicking on a visual element that *isn't* actually interactive (a discoverability failure per L20 — the design "looks clickable" but isn't), or a funnel could show 40% of users abandoning at a specific step of checkout — signals about the *experience* that have nothing to do with whether the underlying API calls succeeded quickly. But these UX tools have no visibility into *why* a technical failure occurred — they can show that users abandoned at a step, but not that the abandonment was actually caused by a slow downstream `AccountService` call that Jaeger would have flagged immediately.

**Why both are needed together:** a purely technical view (Jaeger) can miss real UX problems that occur even when the system is functioning "correctly" by every technical measure; a purely UX-analytics view (heatmaps/funnels) can observe *that* users are struggling without being able to diagnose *why* at a systems level if the root cause is technical (e.g. hidden latency, an intermittent backend error not surfaced clearly in the UI). The lecture placing both tool categories together under Monitor reflects exactly this: closing the DevOps loop requires understanding both whether the system is technically healthy *and* whether real users are actually succeeding at their goals — neither lens alone gives the complete picture.

techQuestions.q: A junior developer says: "DevSecOps just means the security team reviews the code before each release." Critique this statement using the lecture's actual definition of DevSecOps and the CVE/SAST/DAST/secret-scanning tooling described.
techQuestions.answer:
This statement describes something closer to a traditional, siloed security review gate — which is closer to the *opposite* of what the lecture defines DevSecOps as being.

**What's wrong with the statement:**
1. **"Just before each release" contradicts "throughout the loop."** The lecture is explicit that DevSecOps means security is integrated across Plan, Code, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate, *and* Monitor — not concentrated into a single review that happens right before release. A pre-release-only review means a vulnerability introduced early in development sits undetected through Plan, Code, Build, and Test, only potentially being caught at the very last gate — the opposite of the "shift left" principle the build-time CVE warnings demonstrate.
2. **"The security team reviews" implies a manual, human-gated, separate-team process** — but the lecture's actual examples (NuGet's automatic build-time CVE warnings, SAST scanning code, DAST scanning a running system, secret scanning on commits) are all **automated tooling embedded directly into the same pipeline developers already use**, not a separate manual review performed by a different team at a separate point in the process. The whole premise of DevSecOps, per its name (**Dev** + **Sec** + **Ops** combined), is that security stops being a separate silo/gate and becomes something Dev and Ops teams are equipped to catch themselves, continuously, using tooling — not something exclusively owned and manually checked by a distinct security team at the end.
3. **A single review, however thorough, cannot substitute for continuous automated checks.** A human reviewer looking at a diff before release is unlikely to manually re-verify every transitive dependency against the CVE database (the exact thing the automated NuGet warning does automatically on every single build) or manually attempt every OWASP Top 10 attack pattern against a live running instance (what automated DAST does systematically). These are precisely the kinds of exhaustive, repetitive checks that don't scale as a manual, periodic human task, but do scale as automated tooling running on every build/release.

**A more accurate framing:** DevSecOps means security tooling (dependency/CVE scanning, SAST, DAST, secret scanning) is embedded as automated, continuous checks running throughout the pipeline that Dev and Ops teams themselves interact with directly (e.g. a developer seeing a build warning), supplemented — not replaced — by human security expertise, rather than security being solely a separate team's manual, end-of-cycle gate.
